name: Trigeminal Neuralgia

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: ICHD-3 (International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition) / IASP Criteria

criteria.description: Recurrent paroxysms of unilateral facial pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, lasting fractions of a second to 2 minutes
Pain has at least one of: intense, sharp, superficial, stabbing; or precipitated by innocuous stimuli (trigger zones/factors)
Pain is stereotyped in the individual patient
No clinically evident neurological deficit (for classical TN)
MRI demonstrates neurovascular compression at trigeminal root entry zone with morphological changes (for classical TN with neurovascular compression)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Recurrent unilateral paroxysms of facial pain in trigeminal distribution with characteristic quality and triggers, not better accounted for by another diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Three categories: classical (neurovascular compression), secondary (MS, tumor, etc.), and idiopathic (no cause identified). V2 (maxillary) and V3 (mandibular) divisions most commonly affected. V1 (ophthalmic) alone is less common and should prompt evaluation for secondary causes.

laboratory: Blood tests to exclude systemic causes if clinically indicated
imaging: MRI brain with dedicated trigeminal nerve protocol (CISS/FIESTA sequences)
MRI: neurovascular compression at trigeminal root entry zone (superior cerebellar artery most common offender)
MRI: morphological changes of trigeminal nerve (atrophy, displacement) at compression site
MRI: exclude secondary causes (cerebellopontine angle tumor, MS plaque, AVM)
genetic: Rare familial cases reported (autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance)
No established causative genes for most cases
other: Response to carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is diagnostically supportive (positive predictive value >70%)
Trigeminal reflexes (blink reflex) may show abnormalities
Neurological examination: typically normal in classical TN; deficits suggest secondary cause

distinguishingFeatures: MS-associated TN often affects younger patients (<40)
MS has other neurological signs and MRI white matter lesions
MS-associated TN caused by pontine demyelinating plaque
Trigeminal neuropathy has persistent (not paroxysmal) pain
Trigeminal neuropathy has sensory loss on exam
Often associated with connective tissue disease or tumor infiltration
Cluster headache has prominent autonomic features (tearing, nasal congestion, ptosis)
Cluster headache attacks last 15-180 minutes (much longer than TN)
Cluster headache affects V1 distribution primarily

redFlags: Onset before age 40 should prompt evaluation for MS or structural lesion
Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia suggests MS or other secondary cause
Sensory deficit on examination indicates secondary trigeminal neuralgia requiring MRI
Isolated V1 (ophthalmic) involvement is atypical and warrants imaging
Progressive symptoms without remission periods suggest secondary cause or malignancy
Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are first-line; failure to respond should prompt reconsideration of diagnosis
references: Cruccu G, et al. Trigeminal neuralgia: new classification and diagnostic grading for practice and research. Neurology. 2016;87(2):220-228.
Bendtsen L, et al. European Academy of Neurology guideline on trigeminal neuralgia. Eur J Neurol. 2019;26(6):831-849.
Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition. Cephalalgia. 2018;38(1):1-211.
Maarbjerg S, et al. Trigeminal neuralgia - diagnosis and treatment. Cephalalgia. 2017;37(7):648-657.
